title: 5 Things You Can See Tonight Without a Telescope
alt_titles: Your Eyes Can See 2.5 Million Light-Years. Here's How
5 Naked-Eye Sights and How Far Away They Really Are
description_intro: Five things anyone can find in the night sky in about ten minutes, with no telescope, and how far away each one really is: the Moon, Jupiter or Saturn, the Pleiades, the Orion Nebula with Betelgeuse, and the Andromeda Galaxy. Every number comes from NASA fact sheets and NASA Hubble pages.
tags: what can you see without a telescope

sources.title: NASA Space Place: What is a light-year?
NASA Space Place: How far away is the Moon?

beats.say: How far can your naked eye really see? Much farther than most people guess, and you can check it tonight.
By the end you'll know five things anyone can find in about ten minutes, with no telescope, and how far away each one is.
The nearest one is about 384,400 kilometers away. The farthest is about 2.5 million light-years away.
So here is a quick guess before we start. Which of the five do you think is the farthest thing your eyes can reach?
First, the ruler we will use. A light-year is the distance light travels in one Earth year: about 9 trillion kilometers.
Light moves at about 300,000 kilometers per second. Even at that speed, the night sky always shows you the past.
Even daylight is old. The Sun's light takes about 8.3 minutes to reach us, so you always see the Sun as it was.
The farther away an object is, the older the light that lands in your eyes tonight.
So every object on this list is also a time machine, each one with a different delay.
We start with the easiest one of all. What could be simpler than the Moon? Yet its numbers are stranger than they look.
Object one is the Moon, and it is much farther away than most drawings make it look.
It is an average of 384,400 kilometers away. According to NASA, 30 Earth-sized planets could fit in that gap.
And the distance is not fixed. According to NASA's fact sheet, it roughly ranges from 357,000 to 407,000 kilometers.
Moonlight is sunlight bouncing off grey rock, and it needs about 1.3 seconds to cross that gap and reach you.
At full Moon, its mean apparent visual magnitude is about -12.74. That is the brightest thing in the night sky.
Keep one rule in mind for the rest of the list: on the magnitude scale, the lower the number, the brighter the object.
Now look at the dark patches. Those maria are impact basins that were filled with lava between 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago.
The bright highlands around them are older crust. One crater there, Tycho, is more than 85 kilometers wide.
Here is a question for the comments. Before today, how far away did you think the Moon was?
beats.ask: How far away did you think the Moon was?

beats.say: So far: the Moon, about 384,400 kilometers and 1.3 light-seconds away. Next comes a light that is not a star at all. But which one?
Object two is a planet. When Jupiter is in your sky, it looks like a very bright point of light.
At its best, Jupiter reaches an apparent visual magnitude of -2.94, according to NASA's Jupiter fact sheet.
Its distance from us changes a lot, because both planets move. The minimum is 588.5 million kilometers, the maximum 968.5 million.
Even at its closest, Jupiter's light needs about 33 minutes to reach you.
Compare that with the Moon's 1.3 seconds. The Jupiter you see tonight left the planet over half an hour ago.
And it is enormous. Jupiter's equatorial radius is 71,492 kilometers, about 11 times Earth's.
Saturn can take the planet slot too. With its rings, its maximum apparent visual magnitude is -0.55.
Saturn is much farther away: between 1205.5 and 1658.6 million kilometers from Earth.
NASA's fact sheets list 95 natural satellites for Jupiter and 274 for Saturn. That is a lot of company out there.
So which planet will you catch first, the bright giant or the ringed one?
Planets live inside our Solar System. The next object is a family of real stars, hundreds of light-years away. But how far, exactly?
Object three is the Pleiades, also called the Seven Sisters, an open star cluster in the constellation Taurus.
NASA describes it as easy to see with the unaided eye: a small, tight group of stars.
It sits roughly 445 light-years from Earth, though NASA notes that this number is not universally agreed upon.
So the light you see from it set off about 445 years before it reaches your eye tonight.
The cluster contains over a thousand stars loosely bound by gravity, but a handful of bright members dominate the view.
Its apparent magnitude is 1.6, much fainter than Jupiter, yet easy to spot from a relatively dark site.
Galileo Galilei was the first to observe the Pleiades through a telescope. You can do it with nothing at all.
According to NASA, the best time to observe it is December. How many of its stars can you count from where you live?
If you want a map for nights like this, our beginner's stargazing guide LOOK UP shows you where to look. The link is in the description.
So far: the Moon at 1.3 light-seconds, Jupiter at more than half a light-hour, the Pleiades at about 445 light-years. But the next one is not even a star.
Object four hides in one of the best known patterns in the sky: Orion. Look just below Orion's belt.
There sits Messier 42, the Orion Nebula. According to NASA, you can spot it with the unaided eye from a dark sky site.
It is only 1,500 light-years away, the closest large star-forming region to Earth.
Its apparent magnitude is about 4, fainter than the Pleiades, so give your eyes a few minutes in the dark.
It is a stellar nursery: an enormous cloud of dust and gas where vast numbers of new stars are being forged.
Hubble's sharpest view of it used 520 different exposures, and the mosaic holds over one billion pixels.
At its heart, four massive young stars called the Trapezium shape the nebula and carve a cavity with ultraviolet light.
Orion also holds Betelgeuse, an aging red supergiant about 725 light-years away.
It is so big that, if it replaced the Sun, its surface would extend past the orbit of Jupiter. Can you picture that?
Betelgeuse dimmed in late 2019. But that dimming really happened around the year 1300. Its light only just arrived.
Hundreds of light-years, then 1,500. Yet the last object breaks the scale completely.
Object five is the Andromeda Galaxy, the nearest major galaxy to our own Milky Way.
NASA puts it at about 2.5 million light-years away. It is by far the farthest object on our list.
A century ago, Edwin Hubble showed that this spiral was far outside our galaxy, roughly 25 Milky Way diameters away.
Its light left Andromeda about 2.5 million years ago. You are seeing the galaxy as it was back then.
With an apparent magnitude of 3.1, according to NASA, it can be seen with the naked eye, even with moderate light pollution.
On a very clear autumn night it looks like a faint cigar-shaped glow, roughly as wide as the Moon appears.
That faint glow holds an estimated 1 trillion stars. Hubble can resolve more than 200 million of them.
And this is its season: according to NASA, Andromeda is best observed in November. Have you ever seen it with your own eyes?
Hubble's portrait of it needed over 1,000 orbits, spanning more than a decade.
The first known report comes from the Persian astronomer al-Sufi, in The Book of Fixed Stars from the year 964.
Five objects, five distances: 384,400 kilometers, then millions of kilometers, then 445, 1,500 and 2.5 million light-years. So what do you do tonight?
Here is the ten-minute plan. Start with the Moon if it is up, then look for Jupiter or Saturn.
Find Orion's belt, then drop your eyes just below it for the fuzzy Orion Nebula.
Then find the small, tight group of the Pleiades in Taurus.
Finish with Andromeda, the faint smudge that is best observed in November.
Remember the delays: 1.3 seconds for the Moon, about 33 minutes for Jupiter, 1,500 years for the Orion Nebula.
That is about 2.5 million light-years in one glance, and every light-year is about 9 trillion kilometers.
No telescope, no app, no cost. Just your eyes, a dark corner and a few minutes of patience.
Which object will you look for first tonight? Tell me in the comments, and tell me what you saw.
